title: Dangling Pointers and Lifetimes

writing.summary: A lifetime names how long a reference is valid, so the compiler rejects the dangling pointer that a C comment could only warn about.
writing.rule: A lifetime annotation relates the output borrow to the input borrows; it never extends how long any value lives.
writing.explanation:
A C function that returns a pointer into one of its arguments documents the relationship in a comment: the result points into `a` or `b`. The caller in the example frees `b` and then prints the result, and AddressSanitizer reports `heap-use-after-free`. Nothing in `const char *longer(const char *, const char *)` carries the fact that matters.

Rust writes that fact into the signature. `fn longer<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` says the result borrows from the inputs and may be used only while both borrows are valid. The compiler then checks every caller: using `result` after `b` has been dropped is error `E0597`, `b` does not live long enough.

Most signatures need no annotation, because of elision. With exactly one reference input, the output borrows from it: `fn first_word(line: &str) -> &str`. With a `&self` method, the output borrows from `self`. With two reference inputs and a reference output there is no default, so rustc asks with `E0106`, missing lifetime specifier, because it cannot know which input you return.

An annotation describes a relationship. It does not make anything live longer and cannot turn a dangling pointer into a valid one; returning a reference to a local, like `return buf;` for a stack array, is still rejected. Choose lifetimes that state what the code really does: if the result only ever points into `line`, only `line` should share `'a`. Tying `prefix` to it as well would force callers to keep `prefix` alive for no reason.
writing.exampleCaption: `longer` needs `'a` because it has two reference inputs; `first_word` has one, so elision ties its result to `line`.
writing.task: Port the commented C functions, keeping the lifetimes in the starter: `after_prefix` returns the rest of `line` after `prefix`, or `None`, and borrows only from `line`; `longer` returns the input with more bytes, `a` on a tie.
writing.success: The result of `after_prefix` stays usable after `prefix` is dropped, a line shorter than its prefix gives `None` instead of a panic, and a tie in `longer` returns `a`.
writing.question: Why does `fn longer(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str` need a lifetime annotation when `fn first_word(line: &str) -> &str` does not?
answers: With two reference inputs, the compiler cannot tell which one the result borrows from
Functions that compare lengths always need annotations
The annotation keeps `a` and `b` alive until the end of `main`
writing.feedback: Elision covers one reference input, and `&self` methods. With two, you state the relationship; the annotation constrains callers and never extends a value's life.

recall.question: Does annotating the return type as `&'static str` make this compile?
recall.answer: No. `'static` claims the text lives for the whole program, but `s` is dropped when `make` returns, so rustc rejects `&s` with `E0515`, cannot return a reference to a local variable. Return the `String` itself to hand over ownership.

recall.question: Which inputs should share `'a` in a function that returns the part of `line` after `prefix`, and why does it matter to callers?
recall.answer: Only `line`, because the result is part of `line` and never of `prefix`. `fn after_prefix<'a>(line: &'a str, prefix: &str) -> Option<&'a str>` lets a caller drop `prefix` and keep using the result; tying `prefix` to `'a` would force it to stay alive as long as the result.

bridge.fromCaption: The result points into `b`; after `free(b)`, printing it is a heap use after free that AddressSanitizer reports.

contrasts.from: Which argument a returned pointer refers to lives in a comment.
contrasts.rust: The signature's lifetimes say it, and the compiler checks every caller.

contrasts.from: Freeing the source while a pointer into it remains compiles.
contrasts.rust: Using a borrow after its source is dropped is error `E0597`.

contrasts.from: Returning the address of a local is only a warning.
contrasts.rust: Returning a reference to a local is always an error.
